headline_insight: No external benchmark or comparator data was supplied with the 2026 Insurance Survey dataset, so every finding in this report should be read as internally referenced to VisionFund's own client base rather than positioned against an industry or sector standard.
paragraphs: This section would ordinarily situate the survey's GEDSI findings against external reference points — national insurance penetration rates, sector-wide gender gaps in microinsurance uptake, or disability inclusion benchmarks from comparable financial service providers. No such data was supplied with this dataset. Benchmark data is therefore not available for any indicator in this report, and we make no attempt to supply one from memory or inference. Where readers encounter a figure in the preceding sections, it should be interpreted as a within-sample comparison — women against men, clients with disabilities against those without, one country programme against another — and not as evidence that VisionFund is performing above or below any external standard.

It is worth being explicit about why this matters rather than treating it as a technical footnote. In the general framing used across the inclusive finance sector — for example by institutions such as UN Women and the World Bank, cited here only as general context and not as a finding of this survey — gender and disability gaps in insurance access are widely understood to be structural rather than incidental, driven by asset ownership, mobility, literacy and household decision-making power. That general framing is useful for interpretation, but it cannot substitute for a comparator. Without one, we cannot say whether a gap observed in this survey is narrower or wider than what a similar client population would show elsewhere, nor whether an apparently strong result reflects genuine programme performance or simply a favourable sample.

No verbatim client quotes were supplied for this section, so no client voice is presented here; the lived-experience evidence sits in the thematic sections that follow. The practical implication for programming is twofold. First, decisions taken on the basis of this survey should be framed as directional and internally comparative, with the absence of benchmarks stated in any onward briefing to donors, boards or product committees. Second, VisionFund should treat benchmark acquisition as a design requirement for the next survey round — identifying, in advance, one or two credible external reference points per priority indicator (particularly women's insurance uptake and disability-disaggregated access), and building the questionnaire so that its definitions are compatible with them. Without that step, successive survey rounds will continue to measure movement against ourselves alone, which is sufficient for tracking internal progress but insufficient for judging whether that progress is adequate.
